blocks.text: Dear Mr. Garcia:

Thank you for asking us to review what {{fact:f:E-2024-001.client}} pays for its reinsurance. The question, as we understand it, is whether the price is reasonable for the risk your company passes to its reinsurers. We would like the answer to rest on your own records, and to be one that anyone who reads our report can follow step by step. This letter sets out the work we will do, the information we will rely on, the people who will do it, and the terms on which we will both proceed. If any part of it differs from what you expect, please tell us before you sign.
The question we have been asked

A reinsurer prices a treaty on its own view of your business. Our task is to form an independent view of the same business and set the two side by side. For each treaty now in force, we will estimate the claims you would expect to cede, compare that estimate with the premium the treaty charges, and identify the terms that move your net cost. Those are chiefly the retention, any commission or allowance the reinsurer returns to you, and the provisions under which the reinsurer may change its rates.

Some related questions fall outside this letter. We will not negotiate with any reinsurer on your behalf. We will not give an opinion on the accounting treatment of the reinsurance, on the reserve credit taken for it, or on the financial condition of any reinsurer. We will not review the legal wording of the treaties. If you would like help with any of these, we will propose it separately.
How we will approach it
The work falls into three parts. We will keep them apart throughout, and the report will present them in separate sections.

items: 1. The data. We will reconcile the ceded premiums and claim recoveries in your records to the reinsurers' statements, treaty by treaty and year by year, before we rely on either.

2. The assumptions. We will study the claims experience of the reinsured business over a recent period. Where a treaty's experience is too thin to stand on its own, we will blend it with published industry experience and state the weight given to each.
3. The conclusions. We will compare our estimate of expected claims with the premium charged under each treaty, and state what we conclude and why.

blocks.text: Where a conclusion depends on an assumption, the report will say so in the same place. If another reasonable assumption would change the answer, we will show how much it would change.
What we will rely on

Our findings can be no better than the records behind them. We will rely on data and documents supplied by your staff. We will review them for consistency and reasonableness, and tell you what we find, but we will not audit them. To begin, we will need:

items: 1. Each reinsurance treaty now in force, with every amendment and rate schedule.
2. Ceded premium and claim recovery listings by treaty and by year for the experience period, with the reinsurers' statements for the same periods.
3. A listing of the reinsured business in force at the most recent quarter end, showing the amount retained and the amount ceded on each policy.
4. Claim listings for the reinsured business over the experience period.
5. Any rate or pricing correspondence you have received from your reinsurers, including any proposal for renewal.

blocks.text: Files in the form your systems already produce will do. Michelle Banks will agree the experience period and the file layout with your staff when the request goes out.
Standards

We will perform the work under the Actuarial Standards of Practice. Those that bear most directly on it are No. 23, Data Quality; No. 25, Credibility Procedures, which governs how we weight your experience against industry experience; and No. 56, Modeling. Our report will meet No. 41, Actuarial Communications.
The people on the work

I will be responsible for the engagement and will sign the report. Karen Harris, Actuarial Associate, will carry the experience analysis and the assumptions drawn from it, and will coordinate the work from week to week. Michelle Banks, Actuarial Associate, will handle the data, including the reconciliation to the reinsurers' statements and any question about a file.
Day to day, you and your staff will hear most from Karen and Michelle. If anything about the work concerns you at any point, please call me directly.
Start and fee
We will begin work on {{fact:f:E-2024-001.start}}. We expect the review to take about four months. Most of that schedule depends on how quickly the data reach us and how many questions they raise.

Our fee for the work described in this letter is {{fact:f:E-2024-001.fee}}, and it is fixed. It covers the reconciliation, the analysis, a draft report, one meeting with you to go through the draft, and the final report.
Invoicing and payment

We will invoice the fee in two parts, the first when work begins and the second when we deliver the final report. Each invoice is payable within thirty days of receipt. We will not undertake work outside this letter without your written agreement, and any such work will be billed at our standard hourly rates.
Duration and ending the engagement

The engagement runs from the start date above until we deliver the final report and have answered your questions on it. Either of us may end it sooner by written notice to the other. In that case you will pay for the work performed up to the date of the notice, and we will return or destroy your data as you direct.
Confidential information

Your treaty terms and premium records are commercially sensitive, and the claim listings may contain personal information about policyholders. We will hold all of it in confidence, keep it on secure systems, and use it only for this engagement. We will not disclose it outside our firm without your written consent, unless the law requires us to.

The report will be prepared for {{fact:f:E-2024-001.client}}. You may give it to your auditors and your regulators. You may also give it to a reinsurer, provided the report is given in full. No other party may rely on it without our written consent.
Limits on our liability

We will perform the work with the care and skill expected of a qualified actuary. We are not responsible for errors that arise from data or information supplied to us. Our total liability for any claim arising from this engagement will not exceed the fees paid to us under this letter.
Governing law
This letter is governed by the laws of the state in which our principal office is located. If any provision is held unenforceable, the remaining provisions continue to apply.

If this letter matches your understanding, please sign below and return a copy to me. Once we have it, Michelle Banks will send the data request to your office, and we will be ready to begin on the date set out above. We look forward to the work.
Sincerely,

To: Robert Lawrence, Michelle Banks, Nicole Hanna
From: Karen Harris, Actuarial Associate
Re: Reinsurance pricing review for {{fact:f:E-2024-001.client}}: how we are starting

We are ready to start, and the first thing we need is data. The engagement letter has come back signed, and the work began on {{fact:f:E-2024-001.start}}. What we owe {{fact:f:E-2024-001.client}} is an independent view of whether the premiums it pays its reinsurers are reasonable for the claims it cedes, built from its own records. The report will keep three things apart: what the data show, what we assumed, and what we conclude. We should keep them apart in our working files from the first day as well.
How the work is shared

Michelle Banks owns the data. Her first task is to reconcile the ceded premiums and claim recoveries in the company's records against the reinsurers' statements, treaty by treaty and year by year. Neither source is treated as correct until the two agree or the difference is explained in the data log. Nicole Hanna will help with intake while the files come in. She will log each file on arrival and run the first checks on record counts and control totals. Where something does not tie, she will record what she found and pass it to Michelle. No file gets adjusted to make it agree.

I will take the experience analysis. Once the claim listings and the in-force file reconcile, I will build an expected-claims basis for each treaty from the company's own experience. Some treaties will not have enough experience to stand alone. For those I will blend in published industry experience and record the weight given to each, so that the choice can be reviewed rather than reconstructed later. I will also check the rate schedules in the treaties against the premiums actually billed, because an error there would carry into every comparison after it.

Robert Lawrence is responsible for the engagement and will sign the report. He will review the data log before any expected-claims figure is run, and the assumptions before they feed a comparison. Early on I will also put the treaty terms that drive net cost into a single summary: the retention, any commission or allowance the reinsurer returns, and the rate-change provisions. Every result we produce should be read against that page.
Working with the client

James Garcia, the Chief Financial Officer, is our contact at the company. The engagement letter told him that day-to-day contact would come from Michelle and me, and we should hold to that. Every request goes in writing and onto the request log before it is sent. That way his staff are never asked the same thing twice, and we can always show what we asked for and when it arrived.
The coming days

The data request goes out first, because nothing else can move until files arrive. Michelle has drafted it from the list in the engagement letter, and it will go to James Garcia as soon as Robert has reviewed it. It asks for the treaties with every amendment and rate schedule, the premium and recovery listings with the reinsurers' statements, the in-force listing showing amounts retained and ceded, the claim listings, and any rate correspondence from the reinsurers. It also says plainly that files in the company's own format are fine. The treaties need no reconciliation, so I will read them as soon as they arrive and start the summary of terms while the rest of the data are being checked.

We will meet weekly while the data are open, and Michelle will circulate the log the day before each meeting. If you see a gap in the request, please tell Michelle in the next day or two so that it can go out in one piece.
James,

The reconciliation is almost done, and one item on the premium side needs your team's help before we can close it. Your staff's files reached us in good order. Michelle has tied the claim recoveries to the reinsurers' statements for every treaty and every year in the period. The ceded premiums agree as well, except in a single place: for one treaty, the premium shown for the most recent quarter in the {{fact:f:E-2024-001.client}} listing differs from the amount on the reinsurer's statement for that quarter.

We do not yet know which figure is right, and we have adjusted neither. The difference could be a matter of timing, an entry made after the statement was issued, or a correction still to come. Could someone in your finance team tell us which amount was booked, and whether anything has been posted against that quarter since? Michelle can send the treaty and the figures directly to whoever takes it on.

In the meantime we have begun the experience analysis on the claim listings, which does not depend on the premium question. We expect to have the claims side summarized by the end of next week. Once the premium item is settled, we will send you a short note on what the claims show and what we have assumed.
Regards,
Good morning James,

A word on why the quarter in Karen's note matters. Our comparison for each treaty starts from the premium {{fact:f:E-2024-001.client}} actually paid. If that quarter's figure is wrong in either record, the comparison for that treaty is wrong with it.

To settle it, we need the following from your team:
1. The amount booked for the quarter, and the date it was booked.
2. Any entry posted against the quarter after the reinsurer's statement was issued.
3. Any amendment to that treaty's rate schedule that took effect during the quarter.
Item 3 may not apply. I include it because a change of rates partway through a quarter is a common cause of a difference like this one.
Sincerely,
James,

Item 3 on Robert's list can come off. Michelle went back through the treaty documents in your first set of files and found an amendment to that treaty's rate schedule, effective partway through the quarter in question. The reinsurer's statement applies the amended rates from that point on. The {{fact:f:E-2024-001.client}} listing appears to apply the old rates for the full quarter.

That would account for the difference, but it is our reading of two documents, not a confirmed answer. We will not treat it as settled until we have your team's reply on items 1 and 2. If the booked figure does reflect the old rates, it would also help to know whether a correcting entry is planned.
Regards,
Good morning James,
Karen's note on Friday leaves the premium for that quarter open. I do not want it to hold up the rest of the work, so this is how we will proceed until we hear from your team.

For that quarter we will use the premium on the reinsurer's statement, because it applies the rates the amended treaty now carries. That is an assumption, not a finding, and the report to {{fact:f:E-2024-001.client}} will say so. If your team tells us the booked figure should stand, we will rerun that treaty's comparison on it and show both results.

So that the report describes your records correctly, we still need two answers:
1. The amount booked for the quarter, which was item 1 on my earlier list.
2. Whether any entry has been posted against the quarter since, or is planned, and in which period.
Please send them to Michelle when they are ready.
Sincerely,
